ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
In recent years, people have increasingly focused on physical exercise. As shown in Figure (a), there is a fitness equipment called battle ropes, which has a wide range of uses and is often used for cardiovascular or muscle training in the form of high-intensity interval training. During a workout, the mechanical waves formed can be regarded as simple harmonic waves, as shown in Figure (b). A particle located at the origin $O$ starts vibrating at time $t=0$, generating a simple harmonic transverse wave that propagates along the positive $x$-axis. At time $t_{1}=0.3\mathrm{s}$, the wave reaches point $P$. If $x_{O P}=6\mathrm{m}$ and $x_{P C}=9\mathrm{m}$, find:

1. What is the wave speed of this wave?
2. What is the period of this wave?
3. At what moment does point $C$ first reach the crest of the wave?

ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: As shown in Figures (a) and (b), the mechanical waves on battle ropes can be regarded as simple harmonic waves. A particle located at the origin $O$ starts vibrating at time $t=0$, generating a simple harmonic transverse wave that propagates along the positive $x$-axis. At time $t_1=0.3\mathrm{s}$, the wave reaches point $P$. If $x_{OP}=6\mathrm{m}$ and $x_{PC}=9\mathrm{m}$, find: 1. the wave speed; 2. the period; 3. the first moment when point $C$ reaches the crest.
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: In the attached image, a battle rope can be seen being held by a person and forming obvious transverse up-and-down undulations; the rope shape is approximately a sinusoidal waveform, which is consistent with treating the mechanical wave on the battle rope as an idealized simple harmonic transverse wave. The labels O, P, and C are not clearly shown in the figure, but according to the idealized waveform used in the problem statement and the specified method, at the instant when the wavefront reaches P, there are three half-wavelengths between O and P, namely OP = 3λ/2. Then reason: It is known that the wave reaches P at t1 = 0.3 s, and OP = 6 m, so the wave speed v = OP / t1 = 6 / 0.3 = 20 m/s. From OP = 3λ/2, we get 6 = 3λ/2, therefore λ = 4 m. The period T = λ / v = 4 / 20 = 0.2 s. Also PC = 9 m, so OC = OP + PC = 6 + 9 = 15 m. The time when the wavefront reaches C is t = OC / v = 15 / 20 = 0.75 s. Point C needs one quarter period from starting to vibrate to reaching the wave crest for the first time, namely T/4 = 0.2/4 = 0.05 s. Therefore the time when point C first reaches the wave crest is 0.75 + 0.05 = 0.80 s.

The wavefront reaches C at OC/v = 0.75 s. Since a point first reaches a crest one quarter period after it starts vibrating, add T/4 = 0.05 s, giving t = 0.80 s.

method.method_draft: First describe the figure: the rope snapshot shows repeating crests and troughs; in the idealized profile at t1, P is the newly reached wavefront and the nearest crest behind the front is one quarter wavelength behind P, while OP spans 1.5 wavelengths. Compute v from the text: v = 6/0.3 = 20 m/s. Use the visual count OP = 1.5λ to obtain λ = 4 m and T = λ/v = 0.2 s. For the first crest at C, do not first compute C's start time; instead track the nearest existing crest at t1. At t1 this crest is λ/4 = 1 m behind P, so it must travel 1 m + PC = 10 m to reach C. ready3_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: As shown in Figures (a) and (b), the mechanical waves on battle ropes can be regarded as simple harmonic waves. A particle located at the origin $O$ starts vibrating at time $t=0$, generating a simple harmonic transverse wave that propagates along the positive $x$-axis. At time $t_1=0.3\mathrm{s}$, the wave reaches point $P$. If $x_{OP}=6\mathrm{m}$ and $x_{PC}=9\mathrm{m}$, find: 1. the wave speed; 2. the period; 3. the first moment when point $C$ reaches the crest.
